summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. An area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a unit square one way, a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations: you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition), and the product of two nonzero proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part. The whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) folds in as c/d with d = 1: 2/3 of 4 means splitting 4 into 3 equal parts and taking 2 of them, which equals four copies of 2/3. For a whole number greater than 1, the product is larger than the fraction factor (for 1 it is equal, for 0 it is 0).
misconceptions: Leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3), over-generalising the common-denominator rule from addition to multiplication (IES).
Seeks a common denominator before multiplying, importing the addition procedure unnecessarily.
Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).

activities.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
steps: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
activities.insight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.

activities.title: Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
steps: Work out 2/3 × 1/3 on the area grid: shade 1/3 one way, take 2/3 of it the other way, and count the overlap — 2 tiles out of 9, i.e. 2/9.
State explicitly: the answer is NOT 2/3; two-thirds OF one-third is smaller than one-third.

Compare side by side with an addition problem that needs re-partitioning (e.g. 2/3 + 4/5): notice addition needs same-sized parts (a common denominator) before you can combine, while multiplication splits the unit BOTH ways and the b×d grid supplies the denominator.
Explain in words why you do not need a common denominator to multiply.
activities.insight: Multiplication and addition of fractions run different procedures: addition needs a common denominator to combine like-sized parts; multiplication multiplies across because you are partitioning the unit in two directions.

activities.title: Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)
steps: Complete fill-in-the-blank items of the form '2/3 × 4/5 = __/__ = __ (simplest form)'.
Answer a multiple-choice item for 2/3 × 1/3 where '2/3' (denominator left unchanged) is offered as a tempting wrong answer, and choose/justify the correct 2/9.
Finish a problem that yields 6/12 and reduce it to 1/2 as a required step.
Estimate before computing: predict whether each product is bigger or smaller than its factors.
activities.insight: Fluency: multiply numerators and denominators directly, always put the result in simplest form, and expect the product of two proper fractions to be smaller than each factor.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing how (a picture is fine): 2/3 × 4/5, and 3/4 × 2/3. Give each answer in its simplest form.
checkAnswer: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. Multiply numerators and denominators directly (no common denominator), then simplify.
